AI FOR EVERYONE — A SECOND CHANCE TO GET IT RIGHT

The internet began with an extraordinary promise: a worldwide network through which people could communicate, exchange ideas, and share knowledge.
In the 1990s, the World Wide Web was made freely available to everyone. 

One alternative to advertising that we have discussed was a modest annual contribution of perhaps US$10–15 per person. 

That historical estimate still needs verification, and today's costs, particularly for artificial intelligence, would have to be recalculated.
Instead, advertising became a dominant business model. Increasingly, our attention, personal information, and behavior became valuable commodities.

Now artificial intelligence presents us with another extraordinary opportunity.
What if we learned from the internet's mistakes before repeating them?

Imagine an AI system without advertising, financed through a sliding scale: the poorest pay nothing, those who can afford a little contribute a little, and those with greater resources contribute more.
Instead of asking how much money can be extracted from each user, why not ask how little each person needs to contribute to make the system available to everyone?

Such a system would require sustainable financing, independent oversight, and protection against commercial and political manipulation.

But the principle is simple:

Artificial intelligence should serve humanity, not turn humanity into the product.
We have an opportunity to build something better. Why wait until we have made the same mistakes again?

 Eventually, even the wealthy are affected because the entire economic system begins to contract.

Tax the Robots: A Transitional Economic Model

Employees are expensive. From a business pective, robots and AI systems make economic sense because they can dramatically reduce costs while increasing efficiency and productivity.

However, there is a systemic contradiction: The same automation that increases corporate profits may simultaneously reduce the purchasing power of consumers.

If a portion of the enormous productivity gains from automation were redistributed back into society, several things could happen simultaneously:

Companies would still benefit from massive efficiency gains.
Citizens could maintain purchasing power.
The cost of living could be reduced.

Humans Did Not Evolve for Industrial Labor Systems
Another issue rarely discussed is whether modern labor systems are psychologically compatible with human beings.

Humans did not evolve for endless industrial schedules, long commutes, or extreme work cultures such as the Chinese “996” system: 9 AM to 9 PM, 6 days a week.

Such systems create chronic stress, anxiety, burnout, and long-term damage to mental and physical health.

Anthropological studies of hunter-gatherer societies — social groups much closer to the conditions under which humans evolved — suggest a very different pattern of life.
Within communities roughly aligned with the Dunbar number of approximately 150 individuals, hunter-gatherers often spent the equivalent of about 40 hours weekly securing food and necessities.

 However, this was spread over seven days, averaging closer to 5.7 hours per day.
More importantly, these activities were frequently social, cooperative, and meaningful. Hunting, fishing, gathering, storytelling, and tool-making were integrated into daily life rather than separated into something psychologically experienced as “work.”

The modern division between “living” and “working” may itself be historically unnatural.
Automation Could Improve Human Life

Automation and AI also have the potential to dramatically improve quality of life beyond economics alone.

For example, autonomous vehicles could:
reduce traffic deaths,
lower insurance and healthcare costs,
reduce commuting stress,
save enormous amounts of time,
and improve overall public safety.

Combined with robotics and AI-assisted productivity, humanity may eventually move toward a civilization where survival no longer depends upon exhausting labor simply to meet basic needs.

The real challenge is not whether this transformation is coming.

The real challenge is whether humanity managems the transition wisely — or attempts to force industrial-age economic systems to operate in a world where intelligent machines can increasingly replace human labor.

 However, this was spread over seven days, averaging closer to 5.7 hours per day.
More importantly, these activities were frequently social, cooperative, and meaningful. Hunting, fishing, gathering, storytelling, and tool-making were integrated into daily life rather than separated into something psychologically experienced as “work.”

The modern division between “living” and “working” may itself be historically unnatural.
Automation Could Improve Human Life

Automation and AI also have the potential to dramatically improve quality of life beyond economics alone.

For example, autonomous vehicles could:
reduce traffic deaths,
lower insurance and healthcare costs,
reduce commuting stress,
save enormous amounts of time,
and improve overall public safety.

Combined with robotics and AI-assisted productivity, humanity may eventually move toward a civilization where survival no longer depends upon exhausting labor simply to meet basic needs.

The real challenge is not whether this transformation is coming.

The real challenge is whether humanity managems the transition wisely — or attempts to force industrial-age economic systems to operate in a world where intelligent machines can increasingly replace human labor.

There are many additional implications and considerations, but it is important to address one issue at a time to avoid losing sight of the central problem.

Corporate budgets and enterprise buyers are the primary source of financing for the AI ecosystem. While tech giants provide the upfront infrastructure, the long-term tab is trickling down to specific sectors:

Due to "Chipflation" (skyrocketing memory chip prices), hardware electronics like gaming consoles and laptops are seeing direct price increases. Additionally, because AI data centers consume massive amounts of grid electricity, residential electricity rates in high-density areas have climbed, leading to new federal proposals like the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAAJA) to force tech companies to pay the full incremental costs of grid expansions.
2. How Much Does it Cost to Run AI?
The total global infrastructure spend to build and run AI is projected by firms like Gartner to hit nearly $1 trillion in 2026. From a practical operational perspective, the expenses split into two categories:
• The Macro Level (Data Centers): Industry benchmarks show that every single gigawatt (GW) of data center capacity coming online must generate about $15 billion in revenue just to break even on electricity, land, specialized cooling systems, and hardware.
• The Micro Level (Inference & APIs): For individual businesses running AI software, pricing is determined by "tokens" (units of words). While a simple proof-of-concept tool costs around $10,000 to deploy, running custom, highly integrated enterprise-grade AI agents can cost anywhere from $50,000 to upwards of $500,000 annually due to the recurring compute power ("inference") required to handle multi-step autonomous tasks.
3. How Many Chips are Needed?
The sheer volume of hardware is bottlenecking global supply chains, with semiconductor lead times pushing past 40 weeks.
• Data centers are currently devouring 70% of all global computer memory chips, forcing memory manufacturers to pivot almost exclusively to High Bandwidth Memory (HBM).
• To understand the financial scale, Nvidia alone—the dominant hardware supplier—is projected to generate over $206 billion in data center revenue this fiscal year purely from selling specialized graphics processing units (GPUs) and tensor processing units (TPUs) to fuel this demand.
4. How Often Must Chips Be Removed and Replaced?
While  raditional computer processors (CPUs) have historically lasted 5 to 7 years in a data center, AI chips feature a radically compressed lifecycle:
• Physical Lifespan (1 to 3 Years for Training): Because AI models require chips to run at 60% to 70% continuous utilization under high power density (700W to 1400W+), intense thermal and electrical stress causes hardware to degrade rapidly. Experts note that about 9% of AI GPUs fail annually (nearly double the rate of traditional hardware). For heavy-duty model training, a chip's practical physical lifespan is often just 18 to 24 months.
• Economic Obsolescence (2 to 3 Years): Even if a chip doesn't physically break, chip manufacturers are releasing next-generation architectures on an accelerated annual schedule. Newer chips process work vastly more efficiently per dollar of electricity. Consequently, older chips become "economically obsolete" because their high electricity bills outpace their output performance, forcing data centers to rotate them out every 2 to 3 years.
• The "Hand-Me-Down" Strategy: Instead of throwing retired chips away, cloud providers utilize a heterogeneous strategy: they pull 2-year-old chips out of heavy frontier training clusters and repurpose them to handle lighter, less demanding tasks like daily user interactions ("inference") or scientific computing where they can safely run for another 3 to 4 years.
